# Homographies {#sec-homography}

## Introduction

In @sec-geometry_homogeneous we discussed several types of
geometric transformations of two-dimensional (2D) images: translations,
rotations, skewing, scalings, and we saw that all could be modeled as
the product between the coordinates of a point in the input image
described using homogeneous coordinates and a $3 \times 3$ matrix. Now
that we have discussed camera models, we are well equipped to present a
more general geometric image transformation that opens the door to many
applications: the homography.

As we discussed in the previous @sec-stereo_vision, if we capture a scene with two cameras
from different viewpoints, corresponding points across both images are
constrained by the epipolar constrain. In general, there is not a simple
geometric transformation that maps pixels from one image into the pixels
of the other image. To find that mapping we will need to know the
three-dimensional (3D) location of each point as well as the relative
camera translation and rotation between both images.

However, there are a few scenarios where we can find a simple
transformation that allows warping one image into another image
corresponding to a new camera location without requiring knowing the 3D
scene structure: this will happen when the scene is planar (as in
@fig-illustration_homography) or when the two cameras are related just
by a rotation (@fig-rotation_homography). In those two cases the
coordinates of corresponding points across the two images are related by
a **homography**.


:::{#fig-illustration_homography layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/homography/IMG_7801_crop.jpg){width="45%"}

![](figures/homography/IMG_7802_crop.jpg){width="48%"}

These two images are (approximately) related by an homography.
:::

interactions.label: Point Depth
interactions.teaches: Changing the depth of the 3D point moves it along the ray, but its projections on both camera planes remain completely stationary, demonstrating why rotational homography is depth-independent.

interactions.label: Camera 2 Angle
interactions.teaches: Rotating Camera 2 shifts its image plane relative to the ray, changing the projected position (x', y') and demonstrating how the homography mapping updates with rotation.
Allows the user to tilt and orbit the scene to see that these 2D lines represent 3D planar surfaces in space.

demo_steps.title: Shared Camera Center
demo_steps.narration: In this setup, two cameras share the exact same focal center (the black sphere) but are rotated differently. A 3D point (cyan) projects onto Camera 1's plane at (x,y) and Camera 2's plane at (x',y').

demo_steps.title: Depth Independence
demo_steps.narration: Watch closely as the 3D point slides along the ray. Notice that the projected points (x,y) and (x',y') do not budge at all! Because the projections are invariant to depth, we can map pixels between these two rotated views using a homography matrix without knowing any 3D scene structure.

demo_steps.title: Varying the Camera Rotation
demo_steps.narration: Now we rotate Camera 2. As its plane (red) sweeps through the line of sight, the projection (x', y') shifts dynamically. This geometric relationship is mapped precisely by the 3x3 homography matrix defined entirely by the rotation.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Top-down orthographic view looking directly down the Y-axis to match the 2D vector style of the textbook diagram, with a target centered between the camera center and the 3D point.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant green and red camera planes appear as lines, indicating we are looking at a 2D slice of a 3D scene where the plane of projection is parallel to the page (XZ plane). (2) The optical axes and rays run diagonally across the page, indicating a top-down view along the Y-axis (elevation near 90 deg). (3) There is no perspective distortion in the text labels or right-angle markers, confirming an orthographic projection.

camera_view.view_notes: Perfect top-down orthographic view to match the textbook's schematic plane-slice geometry.
